column2: Turkish rendering of the Armenian place name Arkni via Arabic Arghana; a town famous for its copper mine
column3: A town in the headwater region of the Tigris, it appears as Arkni in Armenian sources and as Ergani Madeni ("Ergani Mine") in Ottoman documents; its copper deposits have been worked since the Bronze Age. The Hilar caves and the Neolithic settlement of Çayönü (7000 BC) lie within the district; Zülküf Dağı is held to be the shrine of the prophet Dhul-Kifl.

column2: Armenian jermuk "hot water, thermal spring": from the town's hot springs
column3: A town west of Diyarbakır famous for its thermal baths, its name comes from the Armenian word jermuk meaning "hot spring"; the spa of Jermuk in Armenia bears the same name. Written Çermik in Ottoman documents, the town's Haburman Bridge is an Artuqid work (1179).

column2: From the name of the city Tulukha in Hittite documents; in Roman times Doliche, center of the cult of Iuppiter Dolichenus
column3: The hill north of Gaziantep appears as Tulukha in Hittite texts; in the Roman period the cult of the storm god Iuppiter Dolichenus spread from here throughout the empire. Arab sources called it Dulūk, and Turkish Dülük derives from this form. Its Mithras temple and Paleolithic stone tools are among the oldest traces of settlement in Anatolia.

column2: Greek zeûgma "bridge, yoke": from the pontoon bridge over the Euphrates
column3: The twin cities founded by Seleucus I on either bank of the Euphrates were known as Zeugma, "bridge," after the pontoon bridge spanning the river; the city, base of a Roman legion, is famous for its mosaics. The name of the Ottoman village of Belkıs is linked in popular lore to the Queen of Sheba. In 2000 the Birecik Dam flooded part of the city; the Gypsy Girl mosaic is in the museum.

column2: Arabic iṣlāḥ "correction, reform" + -iyye: from the name of the Fırka-i Islahiye campaign that settled the tribes
column3: Founded as the headquarters of the Fırka-i Islahiye, the army that settled the nomadic tribes of Çukurova and the Amanos mountains in 1865–1866, the town took the campaign's name; Osmaniye was founded in the same campaign. The remains of the Neo-Hittite kingdom of Samal at the mound of Zincirli and the sculpture workshop of Yesemek lie within the district.

column2: A place name explained as Syriac for "high hill"; renamed Aydınlar in 1960, the name Tillo was restored in 2013
column3: The hilltop town east of Siirt bears a name explained as Syriac for "high place"; in the 18th century it became the center of learning of İsmail Fakirullah and his student İbrahim Hakkı Erzurumî. The light mechanism in the tomb, which lets sunrise light fall on the grave, attests to their astronomical knowledge. The town was renamed Aydınlar in 1960 and reverted to its old name in 2013.

column2: Arabic jazīra "island": a city enclosed like an island by a bend of the Tigris, "the island of Ibn ʿUmar"
column3: Founded on a bend of the Tigris, the city was known as Jazīrat Ibn ʿUmar, from the Arabic word jazīra, "island"; in Turkish it became Cizre. The beys of Cizre, the classical Kurdish poet Ehmedê Xanî and İsmail Ebul İz el-Cezerî (the 12th-century engineer) are associated with the city; the Red Madrasa and the Great Mosque are its historic buildings.

column2: Arabic al-Jūdī: the mountain on which the Quran says Noah's ark came to rest; Qardu in Syriac tradition
column3: Named in the Quran (Surah Hud) as the place where Noah's ark came to rest, Cûdî is identified in Syriac and Jewish tradition with the mountains of Qardu; Christian and Muslim sources record pilgrimages to the "place of the ship" on its summit. The Turkish name comes from the Arabic form; the 2114-meter mountain in southern Şırnak overlooks the Iraqi border.

column2: From the Armenian regional name Sasun; the mountainous district in which the epic "David of Sasun" is set
column3: The mountainous region north of Batman is the Sasun district in which the Armenian folk epic "David of Sasun" is set; the name appears in medieval Armenian sources. Written Sason in Ottoman documents, the town was known in the 19th century for its autonomous tribes. The castle of Kozluk (Hazzo) and the highland pastures are the region's natural heritage.

column2: A village name associated with that of the Persian king Darius; the frontier fortress Anastasiopolis founded by Emperor Anastasius
column3: The village southeast of Mardin stands on the site of Anastasiopolis, the frontier fortress founded by Emperor Anastasius in 505 against the Persians; Procopius describes the city's cisterns and walls. According to legend, the village's name comes from Darius's battle here. The rock-cut necropolis and the remains of giant cisterns can still be seen.

column2: Turkish kızıl "red" + tepe "hill": from the reddish hill beside the town; earlier names Arabic Dunaysir, Ottoman Koçhisar
column3: The plains town south of Mardin was a trading center named Dunaysir in the Artuqid period, and its Great Mosque (1204) dates from that era; in Ottoman documents it appears as Koçhisar. In the 1930s the town was named Kızıltepe after the red-soiled hill beside it. The plain, a granary, is called "the wheat field of Mesopotamia."

column2: Arabic Namrūd (Hebrew Nimrod): the legendary king who in popular belief gave the mountain its name; the monumental tomb of King Antiochus of Commagene
column3: The giant-statued tumulus built by King Antiochus I of Commagene in the 1st century BC was linked in popular tradition to the legendary king Nimrod who cast Abraham into the fire, and the mountain came to bear his name; this is a folk etymology. The name Nemrut passed into Arabic from Hebrew. The statues on the 2150-meter summit were rediscovered in 1881; the site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

column2: Origin disputed; the town at the foot of a Commagene-period castle is known by the name of Yeni Kale ("New Castle")
column3: The town that serves as the gateway to Mount Nemrut appears in Ottoman documents under the name Kâhta; the name's origin is not known with certainty and is thought to belong to a local language. The summer palace of the Commagene kings at Arsameia, the Karakuş Tumulus and the Roman Cendere Bridge lie within the district; the Mamluk-period Yeni Kale dominates the valley.

column2: Turkish rendering of the Armenian castle name Behesni via Arabic Bahasnā
column3: The castle of Behesni, which changed hands between the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia and the Mamluks, appears in Crusader and Arab sources; it is written Behisni in Ottoman documents and became Besni in Turkish. The old town was moved from its rocky slope to the plain in the 1950s; it is known for its raisins and grape molasses (pekmez).

column2: Samosata, "the city of Samos," after the Commagene king Samos; birthplace of the satirist Lucian
column3: The capital of Commagene on the banks of the Euphrates was called Samosata after King Samos of the Orontid dynasty; the palace of Antiochus, who built the Mount Nemrut monument, stood here, and Lucian was born here. The center of the Neo-Hittite kingdom of Kummuh was on the same site. Old Samsat was submerged beneath the waters of the Atatürk Dam in 1989; the town was moved to a new site.

column2: Origin disputed; the Turkicized form of a Syriac or Arabic place name, site of the Battle of Nizip in 1839
column3: The town west of the Euphrates appears in Ottoman documents as Nizib; the name is thought to derive from a Syriac village name. The Battle of Nizip, in which İbrahim Paşa, son of the Egyptian governor Mehmed Ali Paşa, defeated the Ottoman army in 1839, was fought here; the young Moltke was among the advisers on the Ottoman side. The ancient city of Zeugma lies within the district; its economy rests on olive oil and pistachios.

column2: The name of the city Adaniya in the land of Kizzuwatna; in Greek legend linked to Adanos, son of Uranus
column3: The oldest form of the name is Adaniya, which appears in Hittite cuneiform texts as a city of the kingdom of Kizzuwatna. Its sound structure has persisted almost unchanged for three thousand years through the forms Greek Ádana, Latin Adana and Arabic Aḏana. Greek mythology links the name to Adanos, son of the sky god Uranus; this is a foundation legend invented later. The Roman-era Taşköprü over the Seyhan River and the Ramazanoğulları principality, which took the city in 1352, are witnesses to the period when the name passed into Turkish.

column2: Hısn-ı Mansur "the fortress of Mansur"; the form Adıyaman is explained by the popular interpretation "adı yaman" (of formidable repute)
column3: The city's ancient core is the Commagene settlement of Perre (modern Pirin). The fortress built in the 8th century by the Umayyad commander Mansur ibn Jawana was for centuries the center of the region under the Arabic name Hısn-ı Mansur. Written Hısn-ı Mansur in Ottoman documents, the name was changed to Adıyaman in 1926; this form is popularly interpreted as "adı yaman," that is, a place known for its fame and toughness. The Commagene monuments on Mount Nemrut are the most magnificent witnesses to the historical layers of the province's name.

column2: Kara hisar (the castle on the dark volcanic rock) + afyon (opium, poppy latex; Arabic afyūn, Greek ópion)
column3: The castle on the city's 226-meter volcanic rock was known in the Byzantine period as Akroinon; in 740 it was the scene of a great battle between the Arabs and the Byzantines. The Turks called the castle Karahisar, "black castle," for the dark color of the rock; after the building works of the Seljuk vizier Sahip Ata, the form Karahisâr-ı Sâhib became established. Opium, obtained from the poppies cultivated in the region for centuries, was prefixed to the name in the late Ottoman period, and in 1932 the official name became Afyonkarahisar.

column2: From the name of Mount Ağrı (Ararat); the mountain's name is linked to the Urartian / Armenian regional name Ayrarat, but its exact origin is disputed
column3: The provincial capital bore the name Karaköse in the Ottoman period; in 1946 the province took the name of Mount Ağrı, the country's highest mountain. There are two interpretations of the mountain's Turkish name: a Turkicization of the Armenian regional name Ayrarat, derived from the name of the Urartian kingdom, or a direct use of the Turkish word ağrı in the sense "high, lofty." Recorded as Urarṭu in Assyrian sources and Ararat in the Bible, the name has become part of world culture through the legend of Noah's ark. The Old Turkic forms "ağır/ağrı" used for mountains also live on in folk narratives.

column2: Founder's name linked to the Amazon queen Amasis; first capital of the Kingdom of Pontus
column3: Amaseia, the birthplace of the geographer Strabo, lies in the valley of the Yeşilırmak surrounded by the rock-cut tombs of the kings of Pontus. Strabo connects the name to the Amazon queen Amasis; this is a foundation legend, and the name is thought to belong to a pre-Greek Anatolian language. Continuing through Latin Amasia and Arabic Amāsiya, the name became Amasya in Turkish. In the Ottoman period the city, where princes were trained as governors, was known as the "city of princes."

column2: Greek ánkyra "anchor" (popular interpretation); a Phrygian foundation, probably related to the Hittite city of Ankuwaš
column3: Ankyra, said to have been founded by the Phrygian king Midas, was explained by Greek writers through the word for "anchor," and an anchor was stamped on the city's coins; the name, however, is most likely a Greek adaptation of an older Anatolian name such as Ankuwaš in the Hittite texts. Capital of the Galatians and center of the Roman province of Galatia, the city preserves the testament of Augustus (Monumentum Ancyranum) carved on a temple wall. In Ottoman documents the forms Engürü and Ankara lived side by side; in 1923 the city became the capital of the Republic of Turkey.

column2: The city of Attalus, after the Pergamene king Attalus II Philadelphus
column3: Around 159 BC the Pergamene king Attalus II had the city founded to give his kingdom a Mediterranean port, and gave it his own name. The gate built in the Roman period for Hadrian's visit still stands today. Arab geographers wrote the name as Anṭāliya; when the Seljuks took the city in 1207 they used the form Adalya. The port that Italian seafarers called Satalia is recorded as Antalya in Pîrî Reis's Kitâb-ı Bahriye.

column2: A Georgian place name; the name of the fortress settlement in the Çoruh valley
column3: Built on the steep slopes of the Çoruh River, the city belonged in the Middle Ages to the Klarjeti region of the Georgian Bagrationi kingdom, and its name appears in Georgian sources in the form Artvani. The name belongs to the tradition of settlement names in the Georgian and Laz languages of the region; in Turkish it lost its final syllable to become Artvin. Under Russian rule from 1878 to 1918, the city joined Turkey through the Treaty of Kars in 1921 and became a province in 1936.

column2: From the name of Aydınoğlu Mehmed Bey, founder of the Aydınoğulları principality; Turkish aydın "luminous, enlightened"
column3: Ancient Tralleis was an important city on the border of Caria and Lydia north of the Büyük Menderes valley; Strabo describes the city's wealth and fine buildings. When the Turks took the city in the 14th century they called it Güzelhisar; the name of the principality's founder Aydınoğlu Mehmed Bey was given first to the region, then to the city. Appearing in Ottoman documents as Aydın Güzelhisarı, the name was in time shortened to Aydın alone. The word aydın derives from the Old Turkic root ay, "moon, moonlight."

column2: Greek palaiókastron "old castle"; in Turkish dialects it became Balıkesri
column3: On the ruins of Hadrianutherae, the city Emperor Hadrian founded while hunting in the region, stood in the Byzantine period the settlement of Palaiokastron, meaning "old castle." When the Turks made the city the center of the Karesi principality in the early 14th century, they adapted this name as Balıkesri; in popular tradition the name is also interpreted as "fish castle" (balık hisarı) or as the castle of a bey named Balak. Written Balıkesir in Ottoman yearbooks, the city remained the center of the sanjak of Karesi.

column2: Adapted into Turkish from the Byzantine Greek form Belokome "fair village / white village"
column3: Located in the founding territory of the Ottoman principality, the city was a tekfur's castle known in Byzantine sources as Belokome. Osman Gazi took the castle around 1299; in Turkish pronunciation Belokome became first Bilecük, then Bilecik. The tomb of Şeyh Edebali and the Orhan Gazi Mosque carry the founding era, in which the name was Turkicized, into the present. The city became a provincial capital in 1924.

column2: A thousand lakes: from the countless glacial lakes in the Bingöl Mountains; the old name Çapakçur is of Armenian origin
column3: The city appears in Ottoman documents under the name Çapakçur; this is the Turkish pronunciation of an Armenian place name containing the element -çur, meaning "river." The dozens of glacial lakes on the summits of the surrounding mountains had long led people to call the area the Bingöl Plateau. In 1945 the name of the provincial capital was changed to Bingöl in keeping with this plateau name. The Turkish words bin "1000" and göl "lake" come from the Old Turkic forms bıŋ and köl.

column2: Turkicized form of the Armenian place name Bałeš via Arabic Badlīs; popular legend links it to Alexander's commander Bedlis
column3: Built in a deep valley west of Lake Van, the city appears in Armenian sources as Bałeš (Baghesh); Arab geographers wrote this name in the form Badlīs. Popular narrative says the castle was built by Alexander the Great's commander Bedlis; this is a legend derived from the sound of the name. From the 16th to the 19th century the city was an autonomous khanate under the Kurdish beys of Bitlis; Şeref Han, author of the Şerefnâme, belonged to this dynasty. In Turkish the d sound changed to t, and the form Bitlis became established.

column2: Turkish pronunciation of the Greek word pólis "city"; the Roman name Claudiopolis means "the city of Claudius"
column3: The city in the interior of Bithynia bore the name Bithynion in the Hellenistic period; under Emperor Claudius it became Claudiopolis, and Hadrian's beloved Antinous was born here. In the Byzantine period the people referred to the city simply as "Polis" (the city); the Turks adopted this word in the form Bolı/Bolu. The same element pólis survives in the names Gelibolu, Safranbolu and İnebolu. The Bolu Mountains, setting of the Köroğlu epic, belong to the city's cultural memory.

column2: Thought to be the Turkish pronunciation of the Byzantine-era settlement name Polydorion; the exact origin is disputed
column3: The city on the shore of Lake Burdur lies in the ancient region of Pisidia; Byzantine sources mention the name Polydorion for the immediate vicinity, and the prevailing view is that the city's name derives from it. Recorded in the form Burdur in the Seljuk and Hamidid periods, the city belonged to the sanjak of Hamid under the Ottomans. The nearby ancient cities of Sagalassos and Kibyra are the magnificent remains of the Pisidian layer that preceded the Turkish name.

column2: From the name of the Bithynian king Prusias I; "the city of Prusias"
column3: The Bithynian king Prusias I, on the advice of the Carthaginian commander Hannibal among others, founded a city bearing his own name at the foot of Uludağ at the end of the 3rd century BC: Prusa. Called Prusa ad Olympum by the Romans, the city was known as Prousa in the Byzantine period. When Orhan Gazi took the city in 1326 it became the first Ottoman capital, and in Turkish pronunciation the form Burusa, then Bursa, became established. Evliya Çelebi describes the city's thermal baths and silk markets at length.

column2: Pottery castle: from the pottery production that grew up around the castle built by Mehmed the Conqueror
column3: At the narrowest point of the strait, Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror built Kale-i Sultaniye in 1462; the town that grew up around this castle, which together with Kilitbahir opposite it locked the strait, became famous for its glazed pottery, which Evliya Çelebi also praised. The people called the castle Çanak Kalesi; after the 18th century this name entered official documents as well. The facing shores of ancient Abydos and Sestos are the stage of a history stretching from the legend of Hero and Leander to the battles of 1915.

column2: The name of Gangra, capital of the kingdom of Paphlagonia; it is reported to mean "goat" in the Paphlagonian language
column3: The name of Gangra, capital of the Paphlagonian king Deiotarus, appears in Greek texts; Strabo describes the city's fortress. Named Germanicopolis for a time in the Roman period, the city hosted a church council in the 4th century. Arab sources wrote Ḫanjara, Seljuk and Ottoman documents Kengırı; the form Çankırı, beginning with ç- in Turkish pronunciation, became official in the 20th century. The city's rock salt mines have been worked since the Hittite age.

column2: Thought to derive from the name of the Çorumlu Oghuz community that settled in the region; neighbor to the Hittite capital Hattusa
column3: The city lies forty kilometers from Hattusa, capital of the Hittite Empire, and from Alacahöyük; the name Çorum, however, is not ancient but belongs to the Turkish period. It is accepted that the name of the Oghuz community called Çorumlu, which settled in the region under the Danishmendids and Seljuks, passed to the city. Appearing in Ottoman documents as the sanjak of Çorum, it became a province in 1923. Popular tradition says the name derives from the form "Çoğu Rum" (mostly Greeks); this is a folk etymology.

column2: Turkish "denizli" (having a sea): from the abundance of spring waters, "a place with water like a sea"
column3: The Turkish city founded beside ancient Laodicea appears in Seljuk documents as Lâdik, and in 14th–16th-century records in the form Tonguzlu. It is accepted that this older name came from the word domuz "wild boar," that the people called the city "denizli" because of its abundant water sources, and that the two forms were confused with each other. Evliya Çelebi records the city as Denizli and praises its vineyards. The travertines of Pamukkale and Hierapolis also lie within the province.

column2: Arabic Diyār Bakr "the land of the Banu Bakr"; in 1937 the form Diyarbakır was adopted by association with copper (bakır) ore
column3: The city on the Tigris appears as Amedi in the Assyrian annals and as Amida in Roman and Byzantine sources; its basalt walls date from this period. With the name of the Arab tribe of Bakr, which settled in the region in the 7th century, the surrounding area came to be called Diyār Bakr, "the land of Bakr," and this name was in time given to the city as well. Written Diyarbekir in Ottoman documents, the name was changed in 1937 to the form Diyarbakır, with a reference to the copper mines of the region. The epithet Kara Amid ("Black Amid") comes from the color of the walls.

column2: The city of Hadrian, from the name of Emperor Hadrian
column3: In place of the Thracian settlement called Uskudama, Emperor Hadrian founded Hadrianopolis, bearing his own name, in the 2nd century. When Byzantine Adrianoupolis passed to the Ottomans in 1361, it took in Turkish pronunciation the forms Edrene and Edrenebol, the latter preserving the element -polis; in the end the form Edirne became established. Ottoman capital from its conquest until 1453, the city is crowned by Mimar Sinan's Selimiye Mosque. The Edirne Palace described by Evliya Çelebi and the Kırkpınar wrestling are the city's Ottoman memory.

column2: Mâmûretülazîz "the place made prosperous by Abdülaziz" (Arabic maʿmūra + Sultan Abdülaziz); shortened to Elazığ in 1937
column3: The historic center of the region is Harput, whose name derives from the Armenian Kharberd, "rock castle"; the fortress's name also appears in Urartian inscriptions. The new city founded on the plain in 1862 in the reign of Sultan Abdülaziz was called Mâmûretülazîz after him. In popular speech this long name was shortened to Elaziz; in 1937, at Atatürk's suggestion, the spelling Elazığ was adopted so as to mean "land of provisions" (azık). Harput Castle and the Great Mosque are the witnesses of the old city.

column2: From the Armenian place name Eriza / Erznka; the name of a sanctuary famous for its temple of Anaitis
column3: The city in the Karasu valley rests on the settlement of Eriza, site of the temple of Anaitis that Strabo mentions in the region of Acilisene. Arab geographers wrote the Armenian form Erznka as Arzinjān; in the Seljuk and Mengujekid periods the form Erzincan became established. The city where Rumi's teacher Burhaneddin Tirmizî lived and where Yunus Emre wandered was destroyed in the 1939 earthquake and rebuilt. Marco Polo mentions the city under the name Arzinga.

column2: Arabic Arḍ ar-Rūm "the land of the Rum (Romans)"; from the Seljuk pronunciation Erzen-i Rûm
column3: At the place the Armenians called Karin, Emperor Theodosius II founded the fortress of Theodosiopolis in the 5th century; the Arabs called the same city Qālīqalā. When the Seljuks took the region after 1071, they used the Arabic name Arḍ ar-Rūm, "land of the Rum," meaning Byzantine territory; when the people of the nearby ruined city of Erzen migrated here, the name was also pronounced Erzen-i Rûm, and the two forms merged in Erzurum. The Çifte Minareli Medrese bears witness to the Saltukid and Ilkhanid periods; the Erzurum Congress convened here in 1919.

column2: Turkish "old city": the name of the Turkish city founded beside the ruins of ancient Dorylaion
column3: Dorylaion, linked to the Phrygian king Dorylaos, was an important spa city of the Roman and Byzantine periods on the banks of the Porsuk; in 1097 the Crusaders and the Seljuks fought here. The Turks called the ancient ruins at Şarhöyük "the old city," and this name passed to the newly founded city. In the Seljuk period the region was known as the sanjak of Sultanönü. Meerschaum carving and the tomb of Yunus Emre at Sarıköy are identified with the city.

column2: Aramaic/Syriac ʿēn ṭāb "good spring" (Arabic ʿaynṭāb); the title Gazi was conferred by the Grand National Assembly in 1921
column3: The city's old name Ayntab is explained by the Syriac ʿēn ṭāb, meaning "good spring"; it appears as ʿAynṭāb in Arab sources and in the form Hamtab in Crusader documents. The city's core is the castle near the sanctuary of Doliche (Dülük) mentioned in Hittite texts. Because of the resistance during the siege of 1920–1921, the Grand National Assembly conferred the title Gazi on the city in 1921; Gaziantep became the official name in 1928. Its urban culture, such as pistachios and copperwork, stems from the bazaars that Evliya Çelebi also praised.

column2: A city name related to Greek kérasos "cherry tree"; the word for cherry spread to the European languages from the name of this city
column3: Kerasous, which Xenophon visited with the army of the Ten Thousand, was a colony of Sinope. Pliny relates that the Roman commander Lucullus took the cherry tree from here to Italy in the 1st century BC; Latin cerasus and the English cherry and French cerise derived from it share the same root as the city's name. Called Kerasounta in the Byzantine period, the city became Giresun in Turkish. Hazelnut production and the Amazon legends of Giresun Island are associated with the city.

column2: Turkish gümüş "silver" + Persian hāne "house, works": a silver-mining establishment; Greek Argyropolis "silver city" is a translation of the same meaning
column3: The silver deposits of the Harşit valley had been worked since the Byzantine period; the mining town that the Greek population called Argyropolis, "silver city," took the name Gümüşhane under the Ottomans from the words gümüş and hane. The city, which had a mint in the 16th–18th centuries, shrank in the 19th century as the mines were exhausted, and the settlement moved lower down the valley. The word gümüş, from the Old Turkic form kümüş, has also passed into Hungarian and the Slavic languages.

column2: From the name of the Hakkâri tribes living in the region; it appears as a regional name in Syriac and Arab sources
column3: The mountainous region in the deep valleys of the Zab was known to Syriac and Arab geographers as Hakkāriyya; the name derives from that of the Kurdish tribal community living here. The city was known in the Ottoman period as Çölemerik, while Hakkâri was the name of the sanjak and the region. When the province was created in 1936, the regional name was given to the provincial capital as well. Nestorian churches and the Cilo-Sat mountains are the cultural and natural memory of this province.

column2: Provincial name derived in 1936 from the name of the Hittite land Ḫatti; its capital is Antakya
column3: Assyrian and Hittite texts refer to central Anatolia as the land of Ḫatti and its people as the Hattians; in the 1st millennium BC this name was also used for the Neo-Hittite kingdoms of northern Syria. In 1936, when the Sanjak question was on the agenda, Atatürk proposed the name Hatay to emphasize the region's historical bond with Anatolia. The State of Hatay, founded in 1938, joined Turkey in 1939. The provincial capital Antakya is Antiocheia, capital of the Seleucid kingdom.

column2: Turkish pronunciation of the Byzantine-era name Sparta; it bears the same name as Sparta in Greece, but the connection is disputed
column3: The city in the region of Pisidia bore the name Baris in the Roman period; the name Sparta appears in Byzantine records after the 10th century, and it is debated whether this is connected to settlers from Sparta in the Peloponnese or to a Greek meaning "sown land." In Turkish the initial consonant cluster was opened with a vowel, giving Isparta. The center of the Hamidid principality, the city has been famous for its rose oil production since the 19th century.

column2: A Turkish plant name from Greek myrsínē "myrtle" (murt); from the myrtle groves on the coast
column3: The present city developed in the first half of the 19th century as the port of Tarsus, through the export of Çukurova cotton; its name comes from the myrtle groves on the coast or from a Turkmen clan bearing the same name. The word mersin is the Turkicized form of Greek myrsínē. In antiquity the nearby ports of Soloi-Pompeiopolis and Zephyrion were the region's centers. The province bore the name İçel until 2002.

column2: Turkish pronunciation of the Greek phrase eis tḗn pólin "to the city"; the Byzantine people referred to the capital simply as "the city"
column3: The Megarian colonists who founded the city in the 7th century BC called it Byzantion after their leader Byzas. When Constantine made the city the new capital of Rome in 330, the name Konstantinoupolis became established; the Arabs called it Qusṭanṭīniyya, and in Ottoman documents it was written Kostantiniyye. The Greek population spoke of the capital as "eis tḗn pólin," that is, "to the city"; the Turks adopted this expression in the form İstanbul. Names such as Dersaadet, Asitane and İslambol are Ottoman-period embellishments; in 1930 İstanbul became the sole official name.

column2: From the pronunciation "eis Smyrnēn" (to Smyrna) of the Greek name Smyrna; a city name belonging to the Anatolian languages
column3: The city's name belongs to a pre-Greek Anatolian language; linked to the form Tismurna in Hittite-Luwian texts, the name is tied in Greek legend to the Amazon queen Smyrna. Counted among the cities claiming Homer's birth, Smyrna was moved after Alexander the Great to the foot of Pagos (Kadifekale). The Greek expression "eis Smyrnēn" became İzmir in Turkish; the Aydınoğulları used this form when they took the city in the 14th century. Pîrî Reis maps the city under the name İzmir.

column2: Exact origin disputed; associated with Georgian "gate city" (kari) or with the Bulgar-Turkic Karsak community
column3: The name of the city, capital of the Armenian Bagratid kingdom in the 10th century, appears in Armenian and Georgian chronicles; interpretations link it to the Georgian word kari "gate," to its position as a pass opening onto the Caucasus, or to the Karsak Turkic tribe that settled in the region. The Seljuks took the city in 1064; under the Ottomans it became a frontier fortress. Russian rule from 1878 to 1918 endowed the city with Baltic-style stone buildings. The Treaty of Kars (1921) fixed the border.

column2: Greek Kástra Komnēnṓn "the castle of the Komnenoi": the name of the family castle of the Byzantine Komnenos dynasty
column3: The Byzantine Komnenos family had made this castle in Paphlagonia their family seat in the 11th century; the castle's name Kastra Komnenon became Kastamonı in Turkish. Turkicized under the Danishmendids and the Çobanoğulları, the city became the capital of the Candaroğulları principality. Mehmed the Conqueror annexed it to the Ottoman realm in 1461; Evliya Çelebi describes the city's castle and its coppersmiths. Atatürk proclaimed the Hat Reform of 1925 here.

column2: Latin Caesarea "city of Caesar (the emperor)"; its old name Mazaka is of Hittite origin
column3: The city at the foot of Erciyes appears in Hittite texts under the name Mazaka; capital of the kings of Cappadocia, it also bore the name Eusebeia for a time. In the reign of the Roman emperor Tiberius (AD 17) the city took the name Caesarea; the Arabic pronunciation Qayṣariyya was continued by the Seljuks and Ottomans as Kayseriyye, then Kayseri. The tablets of the Assyrian trading colony at nearby Kültepe (Kanesh) are Anatolia's earliest written documents. One of the Seljuk capitals, the city preserves the Hunat Hatun and Gevher Nesibe complexes.

column2: The Ottoman name Kırkkilise is a translation of Greek Saranta Ekklesies "forty churches"; changed in 1924 to "the land of the forty (saints)"
column3: The city at the foot of the Istranca range was known in the Byzantine period as Saranta Ekklesies, "forty churches"; the Turks continued the name in translation as Kırkkilise. It joined the Ottoman realm in 1363 in the reign of Murad I. In 1924 a change was sought for a name containing the word kilise ("church"), and the name Kırklareli, commemorating the forty saints (kırklar) who fell in the city's conquest, was adopted. The number forty is a sacred number in Turkish folk belief.

column2: Turkish "steppe city": the city in the middle of the steppe; also known as Gülşehri in the Seljuk period
column3: The city on the central Anatolian steppe is associated with the Byzantine-era bishopric of Mokissos. Known in the Seljuk period as Gülşehri, the city was where Ahi Evran, founder of the Anatolian Ahi guilds, settled; his tomb is the focal point of the artisan tradition. The word kır means "steppe, open land" in Old Turkic; şehir is borrowed from Persian şahr. The Cacabey Madrasa and the tomb of Aşık Paşa are the city's monuments of the Turkish period.

column2: The land of Akça Koca: the region conquered by Orhan Gazi's commander Akça Koca; its capital is İzmit (Nicomedia)
column3: The province takes its name not from its capital İzmit but from Akça Koca, the commander of Orhan Gazi who conquered the region in the 1330s: Koca-ili, "the land of Koca." The capital İzmit is Nicomedia, founded in 264 BC by the Bithynian king Nicomedes I; Diocletian made this city the eastern capital of the Roman Empire. The Greek expression "eis Nikomedeian" became İznikmid, then İzmit, in Turkish. The Old Turkic word koca, "old, great," was used as a name and a title.

column2: From Ikkuwaniya in the Hittite texts; the form Ikonion, explained through Greek eikṓn "image, icon," is a popular interpretation
column3: One of the oldest cities of Anatolia, Konya appears in Hittite records as Ikkuwaniya. The Greeks associated the name with the word eikṓn, "image," called it Ikonion and invented the legend that Perseus carried the image of Medusa here. The Arabic form Qūniya was adopted by the Seljuks as Konya; in the 12th–13th centuries it was the capital of the Anatolian Seljuk state. The lodge of Mevlâna Celâleddin-i Rûmî and the Alâeddin Mosque are the city's Seljuk memory.

column2: The city of Kotys, from the name of the Phrygian king Kotys
column3: Founded under Phrygian rule as Kotyaeion, the city takes its name from the Thraco-Phrygian personal name Kotys; Roman Cotyaeum was a bishopric in Byzantine times. Capital of the Germiyanoğulları principality, the city joined the Ottoman realm in the reign of Bayezid I. In Turkish pronunciation the form Kütahiye, then Kütahya, became established. Together with İznik it has been the center of Ottoman tile-making since the 16th century; it is also the birthplace of Evliya Çelebi.

column2: From the Hittite city name Maldiya / Melid; associated with the Hittite word melit "honey"
column3: The Neo-Hittite kingdom of Melid at the mound of Arslantepe is called Meliddu in the Assyrian annals and Maldiya in Hittite texts; a connection between the name and the Hittite word for "honey" has been proposed. The Roman legionary camp Melitene is the Greek-Latin form of the city; the Arabs called it Malaṭya. The present city moved to the vineyards of Aspuzu in 1838, when the Ottoman army was quartered in the old town. Apricot production and the ruins of old Malatya at Battalgazi are the province's identity.

column2: The name of the city "Magnesia," founded by the Magnetes who came from Thessaly; Magnesia at the foot of Mount Sipylos
column3: Magnesia, founded by the Thessalian Magnetes at the foot of Mount Sipylos (Spil), entered history with the battle of 190 BC in which Rome defeated the Seleucid king Antiochus III. The Saruhanoğulları principality took the city in the 14th century and used the form Mağnisa; in the Ottoman period it was known as Manisa, a sanjak of princes. The tradition of mesir paste is linked to the complex of Hafsa Sultan, mother of Suleiman the Magnificent. The Niobe rock and Yarıkkaya are the city's ancient memories.

column2: From the name of Marqasi, capital of the Neo-Hittite (Luwian) kingdom of Gurgum; the title Kahraman was conferred in 1973
column3: The city rests on Marqasi, the center of the kingdom of Gurgum known from its Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions; Assyrian sources use the same name. Named Germanikeia in the Roman period, the city reverted with the Arab conquests to the form Marʿaş and became a fortress of the Byzantine-Arab frontier. It was the capital of the Dulkadiroğulları principality. For its resistance to the French occupation in 1920, the Grand National Assembly conferred the title Kahraman ("Heroic") on the city in 1973. Its ice cream and its museum of Neo-Hittite sculpture are associated with the city.

column2: Mardē "fortresses," plural of Syriac mardā "fortress"; Arabic Mārdīn
column3: The city at the foot of a rocky ridge overlooking the Mesopotamian plain was known as Mardē, meaning "fortresses" in Syriac; the Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus mentions the fortress of Marida in the 4th century. The Arabic form Mārdīn continued through the Artuqid and Ottoman periods. The Artuqid madrasas, the Kasımiye and the Deyrulzafaran Monastery keep the city's Arab, Kurdish, Syriac and Turkish layers alive together. Mardin stonework is the city's emblem.

column2: Turkish pronunciation of the Byzantine-era settlement name Mobolla; a town in the interior of the region of Caria
column3: The town in the interior of ancient Caria appears in Byzantine sources under the name Mobolla; in Turkish the b sound changed to ğ, producing the form Muğla. The Menteşeoğulları principality took the town in the 13th century; in the Ottoman period it became the center of the sanjak of Menteşe, and the province was called Menteşe until 1923. Its chimneyed white houses and Carian rock tombs show the town's two layers side by side. Bodrum, Marmaris and Fethiye are districts of this province.

column2: From the Armenian place name Muš; the center of the region of Taron, its origin explained by the meaning "misty, hazy"
column3: The city on the Muş Plain, watered by the Murat River, appears in Armenian sources as Muš, the center of the region of Taron; a connection between the name and the Armenian word for "mist" is related. Arab geographers wrote Mūş; in Seljuk and Ottoman documents the name continued unchanged. The nearby plain of Malazgirt was the scene of the Seljuk-Byzantine battle of 1071. The city became a provincial capital in 1923.

column2: Persian nev "new" + şehr "city": the "new city" founded by Damat İbrahim Paşa by developing the village of Muşkara
column3: The village of Muşkara in the heart of Cappadocia was the birthplace of Nevşehirli Damat İbrahim Paşa, grand vizier of the Tulip Era. In the 1720s the Paşa endowed the village with a mosque, madrasa, caravanserai and bath, turned it into a town and gave it the name Nevşehir, meaning "new city" from Persian elements. The settlements famous for their fairy chimneys, such as Göreme, Ürgüp and Avanos, lie within this province. The name Nevşehir is a typical example of the use of Persian words to coin city names in Turkish.

column2: From the city name Nahitiya in Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions; Greek Nakida, Arabic Nakīda
column3: Nahitiya, dependent on the kingdom of Tuwanuwa (Tyana), is mentioned in Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions; Byzantine Nakida became an important fortress city in the Seljuk period in the form Nikde. The Alâeddin Mosque and the tomb of Hüdavent Hatun are works of this period. In Turkish the k sound softened to ğ, and the form Niğde became established. Nearby Tyana (Kemerhisar) and the Aladağlar mountains are the province's historical and natural wealth.

column2: Turkish ordu "ruler's headquarters, military camp": the name of the headquarters of the Hacıemiroğulları principality
column3: Kotyora, where Xenophon camped for forty-five days with the army of the Ten Thousand, was a colony of Sinope near the present city. The Turkish settlement grew out of the camp called Bayramlu of the Hacıemiroğulları, who conquered the region in the 14th century; this place was referred to in documents as "Ordu," that is, the bey's headquarters, and the name endured. The Old Turkic word ordu, "ruler's tent, headquarters," spread through Mongolian into the European languages in the form horde. Hazelnuts and Boztepe are the city's emblems.

column2: From the Greek word rhíza "root, foot of a mountain," Rhizaion "the place at the foot of the mountains"
column3: The town on the Pontic coast appears in ancient sources under the name Rhizaion; the name is linked to the Greek word rhíza, meaning "root" and "foot of a mountain," because the city lies where steep mountains descend to the sea. A fortress city under the Byzantines and the Empire of Trebizond, Rize joined the Ottoman realm in 1461. Tea cultivation, begun in the 1930s, has shaped the city's economy and identity. Laz- and Hemshin-speaking communities are the region's linguistic layers.

column2: From the name of the Phrygian-Greek river god Sangarios; the province takes its name from the Sakarya River, and its capital is Adapazarı
column3: The river that appears as Sangarios in Homer's Iliad and in Phrygian legends bears the name of the river god held to be the maternal grandfather of the Phrygian king Midas. The name, which became Sakarya in Turkish, was given to the province created in 1954; the capital Adapazarı takes its name from the marketplace on the island-like ground where it was founded. The Battle of Sakarya in 1921 was the turning point of the War of Independence. In Turkish folk narrative Sakarya is also associated with the Old Turkic word sakar, "white-blazed."

column2: From the pronunciation "eis Amisón" (to Amisos) of the Greek city name Amisos; a Milesian colony
column3: Amisos, founded by Milesian colonists in the 6th century BC, was an important port of the Kingdom of Pontus; Strabo describes the city's position. The Greek expression "eis Amisón" became Samsun in Turkish; this name appears in Seljuk documents in the 13th century, and the Genoese called it Simisso. The city where Mustafa Kemal landed from the steamer Bandırma on May 19, 1919 is the starting point of the War of Independence. The Bafra and Çarşamba plains are the province's farmland.

column2: From the Syriac place name Seʿert; Isʿird in Arab sources, known in Syriac church history through the "Chronicle of Seert"
column3: The city near the Botan River was an important center of Syriac Christianity; the Chronicle of Seert, which recounts the history of the Church of the East, bears the city's name. Arab geographers wrote the name in the form Isʿird; in Ottoman documents it appears as Siird. The city's "cas" plaster houses and the tomb of İsmail Fakirullah at Tillo reflect the intertwining of Arab, Kurdish and Syriac cultures. Siirt became a province in 1923.

column2: In Greek legend the name of Sinope, daughter of the river god Asopos; associated with Sinuwa in the Hittite texts
column3: The Milesians founded the colony of Sinope in the 7th century BC on the most sheltered natural harbor of the Black Sea; legend ties the name to the nymph Sinope abducted by Zeus, but the name may be an older Anatolian name like Sinuwa in Hittite sources. The Cynic philosopher Diogenes was born in this city; King Mithridates of Pontus made it his capital. The Seljuks took it in 1214 under the name Sinob. The Sinop Raid of 1853 began the Crimean War.

column2: Greek sebastós "august" (Latin augustus): from the name Sebasteia, given in honor of Emperor Augustus
column3: The city on the Kızılırmak took the name Sebasteia, derived from sebastós, the Greek title of Augustus, in the reign of the Pontic queen Pythodoris. The "Forty Martyrs of Sebaste" of Christian tradition are associated with this city. The Arabic pronunciation Sīwās became Sivas in the Danishmendid and Seljuk periods; the Gök Medrese, the Çifte Minareli Medrese and the Buruciye are works of the 13th century. The Sivas Congress of 1919 is where the War of Independence was organized.

column2: Tekfur's mountain: from the title tekfur given to Byzantine lords (Armenian tʿagawor "king"); the ancient city was Rhaidestos
column3: The Thracian settlement called Bisanthe was known as Rhaidestos in the Greek period and as Rodosçuk in Ottoman documents. The mountain behind the city was known as Tekfurdağı, from the title tekfur given to the local lords of Byzantium; the word tekfur is the Turkicized form of the Armenian tʿagawor, "king." After the 18th century the mountain's name passed to the city and in popular speech became Tekirdağ. The Hungarian independence leader Rákóczi spent his years of exile here.

column2: Arabic and Turkish pronunciation of the Byzantine-era name Eudokia / Dokeia
column3: The city in the Yeşilırmak valley developed from the settlement called Dokeia or Eudokia, which replaced Comana Pontica in the Byzantine period; the form Dūkāt in Arab sources became Tokat in Turkish. Under the Danishmendids and Seljuks it was one of Anatolia's major trading centers; the Gök Medrese and the Ali Paşa Mosque reflect these periods. Evliya Çelebi describes the city's coppersmiths and vineyards. Nearby Zile is where Caesar uttered the words "I came, I saw, I conquered."

column2: Greek trápeza "table": from the table-shaped plateau on which the city was founded
column3: Founded as a colony of Sinope, Trapezous takes its name from the table-shaped flat hill on which it was built; the Greek word trápeza, "table," is also the source of banking terms similar to Turkish "trapez" and "sofra." Xenophon's Ten Thousand first caught sight of the sea from above this city and cried "Thalatta!" From 1204 to 1461 it was the capital of the Komnenos dynasty's Empire of Trebizond; Mehmed the Conqueror took the city in 1461. The Sümela Monastery and the Hagia Sophia church are works of these periods.

column2: Turkish tunç "bronze" + el "land": "the land of bronze" (1935); the old regional name Dersim is interpreted as Persian for "silver gate"
column3: The region ringed by the Munzur Mountains appears in Ottoman documents under the name Dersim; this name is explained through the Persian words der "gate" and sîm "silver" as "silver gate" and linked to the region's silver mines. By a law passed in 1935 the province was given the name Tunceli, referring to its copper and tin ores; the capital, the town of Kalan, also took this name. Alevi communities speaking Zazaki and Kurmanji form the region's cultural identity. The Munzur Valley is a national park.

column2: From the Syriac city name Urhāy (Arabic ar-Ruhā); the title Şanlı was conferred in 1984
column3: The ancient city of northern Mesopotamia was known by the Syriac name Urhāy; in 303 BC Seleucus I gave it the name of Edessa in Macedonia. Edessa, center of the Abgarid kingdom, was among the earliest cities to which Christianity spread. The Arabs called it ar-Ruhā; the Turkish form Urfa derives from the Syriac name. Popular belief places the spot where Abraham was cast into the fire at Balıklıgöl. For its resistance in the War of Independence the city was given the title Şanlı ("Glorious") in 1984; Göbeklitepe lies within the province.

column2: Written Uşşak in Ottoman documents; its explanation through Arabic ʿuşşāq "lovers" is a popular interpretation, and the origin is disputed
column3: The settlement on the border of Phrygia and Lydia bore the name Temenothyrai in the Roman period. In the Turkish period the town was written Uşşak in Ottoman documents; although this spelling evokes the Arabic word ʿuşşāq, "lovers," it is debated whether the name is connected to the Turkish word uşak, "child, servant," or to a tribal name. Uşak carpets, woven since the 16th century, reached the palaces of Europe; these carpets appear in Renaissance paintings. Uşak became a province in 1953.

column2: From Biainili, the name the Kingdom of Urartu gave to its own land; the fortress city where the capital Tušpa stood
column3: The rock of Van Castle is Tušpa, the capital of the Kingdom of Urartu founded in the 9th century BC; the Urartians called their land Biainili, and the name Van derives from this word. Urartian cuneiform inscriptions carved into the rock and the trilingual inscription of the Persian king Xerxes stand in the fortress. Armenian sources wrote Van, Arab geographers Wān. The Akdamar Church on the lakeshore and the Van cat are the city's emblems; when the old city was destroyed in the wars of 1915–1918, new Van was built to the east.

column2: Turkish yoz "pasture, meadow" + kat "place, layer": "pasture ground"; the old regional name is that of the Bozok branch of the Oghuz
column3: The city is a town founded and developed in the 18th century by the Çapanoğlu family in the sanjak of Bozok; the name is written Yozgad in Ottoman documents and explained as "pasture ground" from the Turkish words yoz "pasture" and kat "place." Bozok is the name of the branch comprising twelve of the Oghuz tribes, and the province bore the name Bozok until 1927. The Çapanoğlu Mosque and the Clock Tower are the city's historic buildings. An Iron Age city is being excavated on nearby Kerkenes Dağı.

column2: Turkish zonga "reed bed, marsh" + -lık: from the reedy cove on the coast; a city founded on the discovery of hard coal
column3: Uzun Mehmet's discovery of hard coal near Ereğli in 1829 turned the desolate coast between Karadeniz Ereğli and Amasra into a mining basin. The cove where coal was loaded was known as Zongalık, from the word zonga, meaning "reed bed" in the local dialect; the name in time became Zonguldak. The ancient port of Sandrake lies in the same cove. The city, a province since 1924, was one of the Republic's first industrial centers.

column2: Turkish "white palace": from the name of the white-stone palace built by the Seljuk sultan Kılıç Arslan II
column3: The city at the western gate of Cappadocia appears in Strabo under the name Garsaoura; refounded by the Cappadocian king Archelaus, the city became Colonia Archelais in the Roman period. In the 12th century the Seljuk sultan Kılıç Arslan II built here a palace and complex of white dressed stone; the people called the city Aksaray. In the 15th century the Ottomans resettled part of the city's population in İstanbul; the name of the Aksaray quarter in İstanbul comes from here. The Ihlara Valley and Hasandağı are the province's natural heritage.

column2: From the castle name Baiberd, containing the Armenian element berd "castle"; Paiperte in Byzantine sources
column3: The fortress city in the upper Çoruh valley was known as Baiberd, a name containing the Armenian word berd, "castle"; it appears in Byzantine documents as Paiperte. Repaired in the Saltukid, Seljuk and Akkoyunlu periods, the castle still stands above the city today. Marco Polo mentions the city under the name Paipurth, with its silver mines. The bey of Bayburt Castle is mentioned in the tales of Dede Korkut; in Turkish pronunciation the d sound changed to t, giving Bayburt.

column2: From the name of Karaman Bey, founder of the Karamanoğulları principality; its old name was Larende (Laranda, of Luwian origin)
column3: Ancient Laranda was an old city of the region of Lycaonia, and its name belongs to the Anatolian languages; it appears in Seljuk documents as Lârende. In the 13th century the Karamanoğulları principality founded by Karaman Bey made the city its capital; Karamanoğlu Mehmed Bey issued here in 1277 his decree declaring Turkish the official language. In the 15th century the principality's name was given to the city, and in the Ottoman period the form Karaman became established. One of the places accepted as the tomb of Yunus Emre is in this city.

column2: From the merging of the names of the villages Kırık and Kale: a city founded around the arms factories
column3: The military factories founded in 1925 east of Ankara, near the villages of Kırıkköy and Kaletepe, gave birth to a workers' town; the town's name, Kırıkkale, came from the merging of the two villages' names. The word kırık comes from the Old Turkic root kır- "to break," and kale from the Arabic word qalʿa, "fortress." The factories of the Mechanical and Chemical Industry Corporation (MKE) made the city grow; Kırıkkale became a province in 1989. The Kızılırmak flows west of the city.

column2: From the name of the Batman River; batman is a unit of weight in use since Old Turkic times
column3: When oil was discovered on Raman Dağı in the late 1940s, the village of İluh on the banks of the Batman River rapidly became a refinery city and took the river's name when it became a district in 1957. The word batman is a unit of weight known in Turkish for centuries; whether the river's name comes from this measure or from an older place name is debated. Hasankeyf, in the valley of the river that joins the Tigris, is the city's historical memory. Batman became a province in 1990.

column2: Explained in popular tradition as Persian "city of Noah" (Şehr-i Nûh); the origin of the Kurdish name Şirnex is disputed
column3: The town at the foot of Mount Cudi is popularly called Şehr-i Nûh, "city of Noah," because of the belief that Noah's ark came to rest on Cudi; this is a folk etymology. The origin of the Kurdish form Şirnex is uncertain. Recorded in Ottoman documents as a kaza of the sanjak of Cizre, the place became a province in 1990. Mount Cudi, the only mountain named in the Quran, is central to the region's beliefs.

column2: Greek parthénios "of the virgin": from the name of the Parthenios River mentioned by Homer
column3: In the Iliad, Homer mentions the Paphlagonian allies "on the banks of the river Parthenios"; the name of this river, dedicated to Artemis, means "virgin river." The town ten kilometers inland from the river's mouth took its name from the river and became Bartın in Turkish. Attached together with Amasra to the sanjak of Bolu in the Ottoman period, Bartın became a province in 1991. The wooden houses of Bartın and the small shipyards on the river are the city's identity.

column2: From the name of the region and fortress recorded in Georgian sources as Artaani
column3: The high plateau at the headwaters of the Kura River is called Artaani in medieval Georgian chronicles; Armenian sources write Artahan. The fortress passed to the Ottomans in the 16th century and became the center of the eyalet of Çıldır. Under Russian rule from 1878, Ardahan joined Turkey through the Treaty of Kars in 1921 and became a province in 1992. In Turkish pronunciation the t sound changed to d; Lake Çıldır is the province's emblem.

column2: From the name of the Iğdır (Yigdir) tribe, one of the twenty-four Oghuz tribes; it appears in Kâşgarlı Mahmud's list
column3: The city in the Aras valley takes its name from the tribe of Iğdır Bey, held to be a grandson of Oghuz Khan; it is counted among the Oghuz tribes under the name Yigdir in the Dîvânu Lugâti't-Türk, written by Kâşgarlı Mahmud in 1072. There are villages in Anatolia bearing the same tribal name. The region, which changed hands between the Ottomans and Iran, came under Russian rule in 1828, joined Turkey in 1920 and became a province in 1992. It lies at the easternmost tip of Turkey, at the northern foot of Mount Ağrı (Ararat).

column2: Turkish yalı "shore" (Greek yialós) + ova "plain": coastal plain; the Ottoman name was Yalakâbâd
column3: Known in antiquity for the hot springs of Pythia Therma, the region was in the Byzantine period the port town of Pylai, "gates." In Ottoman documents the area appears in the form Yalakâbâd; the name is explained as a compound of yalı, which passed into Turkish from Greek yialós "shore," and ova "plain." After 1929 Atatürk developed the thermal baths and had a mansion built in the town; the Walking Mansion (Yürüyen Köşk) dates from this period. Yalova became a province in 1995.

column2: Turkish kara "black" + bük "wooded thicket in a river bend": a dark wooded river bend
column3: The village of Karabük, thirteen households at the confluence of the Soğanlı and Araç streams, was transformed within a few years into an industrial city by the iron and steel works whose foundations were laid in 1937. The word bük means "dense woodland or thicket on a stream bank" in Turkish, while kara denotes the dark-colored forest. In Ottoman-period documents the village is recorded as belonging to the kaza of Safranbolu. Karabük became a province in 1995; Safranbolu is a district of this province.

column2: Origin disputed; associated with the place name Kilizi/Kilis in Assyrian sources or with the Arabic form Killiz
column3: The Kilis Plain north of Aleppo is an agricultural region settled since the Assyrian period; a connection between the name and the settlement of Kilizi in the Assyrian annals has been proposed, but the evidence is not conclusive. Appearing in Arab sources in the form Killiz, the town was a kaza of the eyalet of Aleppo in the Ottoman period and the homeland of the Canbolat family. Kilis became a province in 1995. Olive oil and the Kilis tava dish are the city's cultural emblems.

column2: Osman, the name of the Ottoman dynasty (Arabic ʿUthmān) + the Arabic relational suffix -iyye: "belonging to the Ottomans"
column3: When the nomadic tribes of eastern Çukurova were settled by the Fırka-i Islahiye campaign of 1865–1866, a new town was founded in the sanjak of Cebel-i Bereket and named Osmaniye after the dynasty. The name Osman comes from Arabic ʿUthmān, and the suffix -iye from the Arabic relational suffix; many Ottoman towns, such as Reşadiye and Aziziye, were named on the same pattern. Nearby Karatepe-Aslantaş is famous for the bilingual inscriptions of the Neo-Hittite king Azatiwada. Osmaniye became a province in 1996.

column2: Turkish düz "flat" + -ce: "flat place, plain"; from the marketplace on the Düzce Plain
column3: The flat plain watered by the Melen River was known for a marketplace that appears in Ottoman documents under the name Düzce Pazarı; the Turkish word düz comes from the Old Turkic form tüz, and the suffix -ce adds a diminutive or locative sense. In antiquity the city of Prusias ad Hypium, founded by the Bithynian king Prusias, stood at Konuralp on the north of the plain; its theater still stands today. After the earthquakes of 1999 Düzce became a province in the same year.
